1. This revision petition is directed against the order dated 16.12.2025 passed by Ld. JMFC-11, West District, Tis Hazari Courts, C.R. No. 52/2026 Page No. 1 of 7 Madhu Sharma v. State Delhi whereby the application under section 311 Cr.P.C filed on behalf of the petitioner/ accused was dismissed.
2. The petitioner/ accused is facing trial for the offences under section 420/ 174-A IPC.

sentences.text:
The statement of the accused under section 313 Cr.P.C. was recorded before the Ld. Trial Court on 26.05.2025 and thereafter the matter was fixed for defence evidence on 16.07.2025, 11.08.2025,
26.08.2025, 16.09.2025 and 28.10.2025 and ultimately on 28.10.2025 the opportunity of the petitioner/ accused to lead defence evidence was closed as she failed to lead defence evidence despite repeated adjournments.
Thereafter, on 16.11.2025 an application under section 311 Cr.P.C was filed on behalf of the petitioner/ accused seeking permission to lead defence evidence.

The said application was also dismissed by the Ld. Trial Court vide order dated 16.12.2025 on the premise that sufficient opportunities had been granted to the petitioner/ accused to lead defence evidence and thereafter defence evidence was closed by a reasoned order dated 28.10.2025 and that no medical documents had been filed by the accused and that change of counsel can not be taken as a circumstance beyond the control of the accused.

sentences.text: 3. The petitioner/ accused has assailed the orders dated 28.10.2025 and 16.11.2025 by way of the present revision petition.
4. Ld.

Counsel for the petitioner/ accused has argued that the closure of defence evidence would cause irreparable prejudice to the petitioner/ accused and no substantial prejudice would be caused to the Madhu v. State prosecution in case the petitioner/ accused is permitted to lead defence evidence.
It has been further submitted that the petitioner/ accused has already deposited costs of Rs. 2500/- imposed by the Ld. Trial Court.
It has been further submitted that the defence evidence could not be led on account of change of counsel.
He has accordingly prayed that the impugned orders dated 28.10.2025 and 16.11.2025 be set aside and the petitioner/ accused be permitted to lead defence evidence.

5. On the other hand, Ld. Addl. P.P for the State has opposed the revision petition and the contentions raised by the Ld. Counsel for the petitioner/ accused and has argued that sufficient opportunities were given to the petitioner/ accused to lead defence evidence and since the petitioner/ accused failed to lead defence evidence so the right of the petitioner/ accused to lead defence evidence was rightly closed.
He has further argued that the impugned orders are interlocutory orders and therefore revision is not maintainable.
He has, accordingly, prayed for dismissal of the present revision petition.
6. Ld.

Counsel for the the petitioner/ accused has further argued that the right of the the petitioner/
accused to lead DE was closed and thereafter the application under section 311 Cr.P.C. for reopening of the same has also been dismissed and therefore the impugned orders cannot be said to be interlocutory orders and thus the present revision is maintainable.

I have heard the Ld. Counsel for the petitioner/ accused and the Ld. Addl. P.P. for the State.
8.

The first question to be decided by this Court is as to whether the present revision petition is maintainable in view of the bar created by section 397(2) Cr.P.C., which provides that the powers of revision conferred by sub-section (1) of section 397 Cr.P.C. shall not be exercised in relation to any interlocutory order passed in any appeal, inquiry, trial or other proceeding.

9. In the judgment titled as Amar Nath v. State of Haryana reported in 1978 SCR (1) 222 the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that:
"The term "interlocutory order" is a term of well- know legal significance which has been used in various statutes.

entities.text: Amar Nath v. State of Haryana reported in 1978 SCR (1) 222
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Decided cases have laid down that interlocutory orders to be appealable must be those which decide the right and liabilities of the parties concerning a particular aspect.
The term "interlocutory order" in s. 397(2) has, been used in a restricted sense and not in any broad and artistic sense.
It merely denotes orders of a purely interim or temporary nature which do not decide or touch the important rights or liabilities of the parties.

Any order which substantially affects the Madhu Sharma vs State on 3 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/112700690/
2 right of the accused, or decides certain rights of the parties cannot be said to be an interlocutory order so as to bar a revision to the High Court against that order,
because that would be against the very object which formed the basis for insertion of this provision in S. 397 of the Code.

State instance, orders summoning witnesses, adjourning cases, passing orders for bail, calling for reports and such other steps in aid of the pending proceeding, may no doubt amount to interlocutory orders against which no revision would lie under s. 397(2) of the Code.

But orders which are matters of moment and which affect or adjudicate the rights of the accused or a particular aspect of the trial cannot be said to be interlocutory orders so as to be outside the purview of the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court."
10.

In the judgment titled as Sethuraman v. Rajamanickam, (2009) 5 SCC 153 the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held:
".......5.

Secondly, what was not realised was that the orders passed by the trial court refusing to call the documents and rejecting the application under Section 311 CrPC,
were interlocutory orders and as such, the revision against those orders was clearly barred under Section 397(2) CrPC.

The trial court, in its common order, had clearly mentioned that the cheque was admittedly signed by the respondent- accused and the only defence that was raised, was that his signed cheques were lost and that the appellant complainant had falsely used one such cheque.
The trial court also recorded a finding that the documents were not necessary.

This order did not, in any manner,
decide anything finally.

Therefore, both the orders i.e. one on the application under Section 91 CrPC for production of documents and other on the application under Section 311 CrPC for recalling the witness, Madhu Sharma v. State were the orders of interlocutory nature, in which case, under Section 397(2), revision was clearly not maintainable.
Under such circumstances, the learned Judge could not have interfered in his revisional jurisdiction....."

11. In the judgment titled as Varun Aggarwal v. State of NCT of Delhi, 2017 SCC OnLine Del 12364 the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi had held that the order whereby the right of the petitioner to examine the forensic expert was closed as he could not file the forensic report was an interlocutory order as it does not finalise the complete proceedings pending before the Trial Court and thus it was held that criminal revision was not maintainable.

sentences.text: 12. Adverting to the facts of the present case, keeping in view the legal position enumerated herein-above, the order dated 28.10.2025 closing defence evidence cannot be said to be a final order.

The accused moved an application under section 311 Cr.P.C. essentially seeking further opportunity for leading defence evidence, which itself shows that the order closing defence evidence was interlocutory in nature.
The said application was again dismissed vide order dated 16.11.2025.
The effect of the said order is again that defence evidence has not been permitted to be reopened and therefore again the order dated 16.11.2025 cannot be said to be a final order.

In view of the aforesaid judgments, I am of the opinion that the orders dated 28.10.2025 and 16.11.2025 are interlocutory orders and therefore the present revision petition in not maintainable in view of the Madhu Sharma vs State on 3 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/112700690/
